There was no RAD similar to Delphi or Visual Studio (for a brief time there was a Delphi replacement called Kylix which was great but unfortunately was soon discontinued by Borland), all you had was a ton of pretty much unrelated text editors and tools that made things like coding and debugging a real pain in the ass, frequently forcing you to learn command line parameters and shortcuts because ease of use and user-friendliness was always an afterthought.

When you had to install something you better pray it was available on whatever package manager your distro used. As i said, package managers made installing software much easier and contained thousands of libraries and softwares... but what if you needed the latest version of a software? Chances are no one yet made a package for you so you were on your own. And what if you needed a software not available in the package manager? Again, you were on your own. Good luck installing all the required libraries and compiling from source, especially if you don't know C/C++. And what if such software required libraries not provided by your package manager? Again, you were on your own. Installing a software on Windows usually requires you to double click on the EXE file and follow the installer, installing a software outside the package manager of Linux might easily require hours or browsing among hundreds of error lines and browsing the WEB hoping someone else found whatever was the issue. Also, since Linux has the bad habit to put all the libraries used by the installed softwares in a huge folder (a thing that made sense in the old unix days but no anymore with disks measured in terabytes), you could fuck things up very badly by installing by hand a never (or older) version of said libraries that suddenly made other softwares incapable of functioning properly.
